l: Odysseus, Hesiod, the Homeric Hymns, and Homerica
s: Odysseus is a cunning and resourceful son of Laertes whose record follows him from seeking Helen in marriage to his death. He sends Helen no gifts, expecting Menelaus to prevail, and pretends madness to avoid the expedition until the deception is exposed through Telemachus. In the struggle over Achilles’s body he helps drive off Trojans, later wins Achilles’ arms, captures Helenus, and helps bring Neoptolemus from Scyros. Disguised as a beggar in Ilium, he plots with Helen, kills Trojans, and steals the Palladium with Diomedes; after the sack he kills Astyanax. In later travels he sacrifices to the Nymphs, has herds in Elis, receives a mixing bowl from Polyxenus, follows Teiresias’s sacrificial orders, and goes to Thesprotis. There he marries Callidice and leads the Thesprotians against the Brygi before returning to Ithaca. He is father of Agrius, Latinus, and Telegonus with Circe, and Telegonus unwittingly kills him while he defends Ithaca.

l: Aias, Hesiod, the Homeric Hymns, and Homerica
s: Aias is a hero named from an eagle. He carries Achilles’ body to the ships while Odysseus drives off Trojans, then quarrels and disputes with Odysseus over Achilles’ arms. After Odysseus receives them, Aias goes mad, destroys the Achaeans’ herd, kills himself about dawn, and is buried in a coffin because of the king’s anger.

l: Memnon, Hesiod, the Homeric Hymns, and Homerica
s: Memnon, Ethiopia's brazen-crested king and son of Eos, aids the Trojans in Hephaestus-made armour, kills Antilochus, falls to Achilles, and receives immortality through Eos and Zeus.

l: Antilochus, Hesiod, the Homeric Hymns, and Homerica
s: is_killed_by Memnon [in battle] Antilochus is slain by Memnon. The Achaeans bury him.

l: Patroclus, Hesiod, the Homeric Hymns, and Homerica
s: Patroclus carries Lycaon away to Lemnos and sells him as a slave.

l: Sinon, Hesiod, the Homeric Hymns, and Homerica
s: Sinon secretly enters Ilium by pretence and raises the arranged fire-signal, bringing Greek ships from Tenedos and beginning the attack.

l: Philoctetes, Hesiod, the Homeric Hymns, and Homerica
s: Achaean warrior and leader of spearmen, abandoned on Lemnos for a snake wound’s stench, brought back and healed, then kills Alexandrus in single combat and later Admetus.

l: Neoptolemus, Hesiod, the Homeric Hymns, and Homerica
s: Neoptolemus, son of Achilles, is brought from Scyros by Odysseus and receives Achilles’ arms after Achilles’ ghost appears. He kills several opponents, including Priam at Zeus Herceius’s altar, and takes Andromache as his prize. Warned by Thetis, he travels overland, meets Odysseus at Maronea, buries Phoenix, reaches the Molossi, and is recognized by Peleus.

l: Eurypylus, Hesiod, the Homeric Hymns, and Homerica
s: Trojan ally and son of Telephus arrives, shows prowess and kills Machaon, then is killed by Neoptolemus.

l: Agamemnon, Hesiod, the Homeric Hymns, and Homerica
s: Agamemnon, son-in-law of Tyndareus and brother of Menelaus, helps organize an expedition and provides its leaders’ feast. After boasting over a stag, he angers Artemis, who demands Iphigeneia’s sacrifice. Returning from Troy, he quarrels with Menelaus, delays to appease Athena, ignores Achilles’ ghost’s warning, and is murdered by Aegisthus and Clytaemnestra.

l: Menelaus, Hesiod, the Homeric Hymns, and Homerica
s: Menelaus is Helen’s suitor, husband, and the father of Hermione and Nicostratus. He wins Helen by offering the greatest gifts and having the greatest possessions among the Achaeans. After entertaining Alexandrus and leaving Helen in Sparta, he learns what happened, returns, plans an expedition against Ilium with his brother, and visits Nestor. At Ilium he mistreats Alexandrus’s body, casts away his sword on seeing Helen, finds her, kills Deiphobus, and takes her to the ships. After quarrelling with Agamemnon, he survives a voyage to Egypt and eventually returns home.

l: Orestes, Hesiod, the Homeric Hymns, and Homerica
s: takes_vengeance_for Agamemnon's murder [with Pylades] Orestes takes vengeance for Agamemnon’s murder together with Pylades.

l: Aegisthus, Hesiod, the Homeric Hymns, and Homerica
s: Aegisthus becomes Clytaemnestra’s lover after she deserts Agamemnon, then murders Agamemnon with her.

l: Telegonus, Hesiod, the Homeric Hymns, and Homerica
s: Telegonus, son of Odysseus and Calypso, searches for his father, lands on and ravages Ithaca, and unwittingly kills Odysseus. After learning his mistake, he transports Odysseus’s body, Penelope, and Telemachus to Calypso’s island, then marries Penelope.

l: Circe, Hesiod, the Homeric Hymns, and Homerica
s: Circe, a witch and daughter of the Sun, bears Agrius, Latinus, and Telegonus with Odysseus; after Odysseus’s body reaches her island, she makes him, Penelope, and Telemachus immortal, then marries Telemachus.

l: Telemachus, Hesiod, the Homeric Hymns, and Homerica
s: Odysseus’s son Telemachus is taken with Odysseus’s body and Penelope to Circe’s island, becomes immortal, and marries Circe.

l: Persephone, Hesiod, the Homeric Hymns, and Homerica
s: Persephone is a deathless, lovely goddess, Demeter’s daughter and the wife of Hades, also called Aidoneus. While gathering flowers with the daughters of Oceanus, the earth opens and Hades carries her away in a golden chariot against her will; she cries for her father, and Demeter grieves. Brought back to Demeter, she recounts the abduction, but because she ate a pomegranate seed in the underworld, she resides there for one-third of each year and returns to earth for two-thirds.

l: Hades, Hesiod, the Homeric Hymns, and Homerica
s: Hades is a god, brother of Demeter and Zeus, born to Cronos, who swallows him and later brings him forth. Assigned the underworld, he rules the dead from beneath the earth, where his house with Persephone is guarded by a fearful hound. Called Aidoneus and Host of Many, he abducts Persephone in his golden chariot with Zeus’s permission and becomes her husband. When Zeus orders her release, Hades obeys but secretly gives her a pomegranate seed, promising her rule and honors among the deathless gods.

l: the Eleusinian Mysteries, Hesiod, the Homeric Hymns, and Homerica
s: The Eleusinian Mysteries are Demeter’s sacred rites, promised to the people of Eleusis and taught to Triptolemus, Diocles, Eumolpus, Celeus, and others. They must be performed reverently and kept secret, neither transgressed, investigated, nor spoken of. Initiates who see them are blessed after death; the uninitiated lack comparable good.

l: Eleusis, Hesiod, the Homeric Hymns, and Homerica
s: Eleusis, ruled by Celeus, is a place with a rocky stronghold, the Maiden Well, and Demeter’s temple. Demeter arrives disguised, its women draw water, and she commands a temple and altar; after fertility returns, she teaches its rites and mysteries.

l: Apollo, Hesiod, the Homeric Hymns, and Homerica
s: Apollo is a deathless, far-shooting god, also called Phoebus, lord, and Far-shooter. He is the son of Zeus and Leto, brother and foster companion of Artemis, and father of Chaeron. He bears a bright curved or silver bow, a golden blade or sword, and a hollow lyre with golden keys. The lyre and bow are especially dear to him, and he plays among the gods of Olympus with radiant appearance. He alone is permitted to know Zeus’s counsel, declares Zeus’s unfailing will, practices divination, and teaches the three prophetic sisters. Through Apollo and the Muses come singers and lyre-players. Born on Delos after Leto’s long labor, Apollo makes Delos his principal and favored dwelling and reigns over it. There stand his temple and oracle; the Ionians honor him at their gathering, and the girls of Delos praise him before their songs. He is also associated with Lycia, Maeonia, and Miletus, has wooded groves in many places, and waits for Artemis at vine-clad Claros. His holy houses are at Pytho and in Delphi’s rich land. Seeking a place for an oracle, Apollo travels through many regions, establishes a temple and oracle at Crisa, kills the dragoness by its spring, and renames the place Pytho after she rots there. He punishes Telphusa by covering her streams with rocks. Diverting a Cretan ship, he brings the Cretans to Crisa to serve the sanctuary, instructs them, and promises abundant offerings. Apollo’s conflict with Hermes begins when Hermes steals Apollo’s cattle from Pieria. Apollo follows their reversed tracks, questions an old man at Onchestus, finds Hermes in Maia’s cave, carries him away, and brings the dispute before Zeus and the immortals. Delighted by Hermes’ lyre, Apollo exchanges his whip for it, becomes Hermes’ friend, and grants him a golden staff and prophetic privileges. He kills Meleager while Meleager fights the Curetes, slays Hyacinthus unwittingly with a discus, kills Amphilochus at Soli, and is represented as destroying the Cyclopes. He loves Hymenaeus and would not leave Magnes’ house; another account says he loved Ileus. A swan and a minstrel sing of him, and he is invoked to favor song.

l: Delos, Hesiod, the Homeric Hymns, and Homerica
s: Delos is a sea-girt, rocky island with poor soil that agrees to receive Apollo after Leto promises an altar, precinct, and oracle; at his birth it gains gold, supreme honor, and becomes where Ionians gather for the Delian festival.

l: Telphusa, Hesiod, the Homeric Hymns, and Homerica
s: Telphusa is a sweet-flowing sacred spring who deceives Apollo to preserve her renown; he discovers this, covers her streams with rocks, and establishes an altar nearby.

l: Hermes, Hesiod, the Homeric Hymns, and Homerica
s: Hermes is a deathless god, born on Cyllene to Zeus and Maia, and is chiefly the swift, luck-bringing messenger, guide, and herald of Zeus, the blessed gods, and the deathless gods. He serves Zeus, bears a golden rod or staff of riches and wealth, gives grace, good, and good things, and is asked to aid the wisdom and strength of men. He rules or is lord of Cyllene and Arcadia, is associated with Cyllene’s sacred place, and receives authority over cattle, birds of omen, various animals, and service as messenger to Hades. From his first day, Hermes is defined by inventive speed and cunning. Born on the fourth day of the month, he contrives the lyre from a tortoise shell, invents fire-making and pipes, and has sandals woven from tamarisk and myrtle twigs. While still new-born, he steals fifty of Apollo’s cattle, drives them to the Alpheus, sacrifices two, returns unseen to his cradle, and elaborately denies the theft. Brought before Zeus and the immortals with Apollo, he reveals and gives Apollo the lyre; Apollo promises friendship, while Hermes receives cattle-keeping and further powers. Elsewhere he steals twelve heifers, a hundred unyoked cows, and a bull from herds associated with Apollo and Admetus. He tests Battus in disguise, and when Battus reveals the cattle’s location, strikes him with his staff and changes him into a rock. Hermes is repeatedly a robber, thief, cattle driver, night watcher, dream-bringer, and cunning trickster, but also a worshipful and dear divine helper. He uses stupor and strangling upon dogs connected with a stolen herd, and he slays Argus, giving him the title Slayer of Argus. At Zeus’s command he travels to Erebus, persuades Hades to release Persephone, drives the immortal horses, and returns her to Demeter’s temple. He leads Hera, Athena, and Aphrodite to Alexandrus for judgment; carries Aphrodite to learn she will wed Anchises; and tells Tros what happened to Ganymedes. He is also Pan’s father: after tending sheep for a mortal man and marrying the daughter of Dryops, he carries Pan to the deathless gods.

l: Aphrodite, Hesiod, the Homeric Hymns, and Homerica
s: Aphrodite is an immortal, foam-born goddess of love, born from Heaven’s severed members and sea foam, accompanied by Eros and Desire. Golden, beautiful, and crowned with gold and violets, she governs love and sexual desire among gods, mortals, birds, and creatures of land and sea; her portion includes whisperings, smiles, deceits, love, and graciousness. All are subject to her will except Athene, Artemis, and Hestia, whose hearts she cannot bend. Brought by the western wind to Cyprus, she is clothed and adorned there, welcomed by the gods, and becomes associated with Paphos, Salamis, and Cyprus as goddess and queen who gives kindly gifts. Her power can punish: angered when Tyndareus forgot her in sacrifice, she caused his daughters to desert husbands and cast them into evil report. Yet Zeus makes her subject to desire for the mortal Anchises. She joins with him, bears Aeneas, reveals her divinity, is shamed among the deathless gods, and instructs Anchises to conceal their union. She also shapes Alexandrus’s course by promising Helen, suggesting shipbuilding, bringing them together, and ordering Aeneas to sail with Alexandrus. Throughout, she is portrayed as radiant and smiling, but as a force whose desire, favor, and anger direct both gods and mortals.

l: Anchises, Hesiod, the Homeric Hymns, and Homerica
s: Anchises is a handsome mortal herdsman on Mount Ida, descended from Dardanus. He welcomes and sleeps with Aphrodite believing her mortal, fears her revealed divinity, and learns he will father Aeneas if he conceals their union.

l: Ida, Hesiod, the Homeric Hymns, and Homerica
s: Ida is a many-fountained, forested, furrowed, windy mountain, rich in wild creatures and Nymphs, where Anchises tends cattle, Aphrodite finds him, and Nymphs raise Aeneas.

l: Artemis, Hesiod, the Homeric Hymns, and Homerica
s: Artemis is a goddess, virgin and pure maiden, daughter of Leto and Zeus, and sister and foster-companion of Apollo. An arrow-loving huntress, she delights in archery and the chase, shoots stags, hunts wild beasts, cheers hounds, and bears a golden curved bow and grievous golden-shafted arrows. She has horses and an all-golden chariot, travels through Smyrna to Claros, and at Delphi sets aside her weapons to lead the dances of the Muses and Graces. She accompanies Callisto in mountain hunting, angrily changes the pregnant Callisto into a bear, and later prays with Leto for Orion. When Agamemnon kills a stag and boasts against her, she stops the Greeks with winds; after Iphigeneia is brought for sacrifice, she removes her, takes her to the Tauri, makes her immortal, and leaves a stag instead.

l: Athena, Hesiod, the Homeric Hymns, and Homerica
s: Athena is a bright-eyed, grey-eyed, queenly, host-leading, battle-loving goddess: daughter of Zeus, holder of a dark aegis and a host-scaring weapon, and equal to Zeus in strength and wise understanding. Destined as Metis’s very wise daughter, she is born from Zeus’s head already armed for war and resides with him on Olympus. She delights in Ares, wars, and battle-craft, yet confronts him when he fights Heracles: she encourages Heracles and Iolaus, conveys Zeus’s grant of power against Cycnus, instructs Heracles how to wound Ares, rides with them, warns Ares, and turns aside his spear. With Hephaestus she teaches men glorious gifts. She disputes fairness with Aphrodite, is judged among three goddesses by Alexandrus, and polishes Peleus’s spear. In the struggle around Troy, she helps Odysseus gain Achilles’ arms, directs Epeius in building the wooden horse, receives the Trojans’ dedication of it, and is angered by Aias’s treatment of her image and Cassandra; she plans destruction for the departing Greeks and causes Agamemnon and Menelaus to quarrel. Finally, offended by damage to her temple possessions and by the Frogs’ noise, she refuses aid to both Mice and Frogs and tells the gods to watch their battle.

l: Hestia, Hesiod, the Homeric Hymns, and Homerica
s: Hestia is a pure maiden and queenly goddess, daughter of Cronos, described as both first-born and youngest child. She refuses Poseidon and Apollo in marriage, and Zeus grants her high honour instead. She tends Apollo’s holy house at Pytho, shares one mind with Zeus, and has an everlasting abode among deathless gods and people on earth. Her honour, portion, and right are glorious. No mortal banquet occurs without her: sweet wine is offered first and last. Invited to dwell with Hermes, she bestows grace and aids people’s wisdom and strength.

l: Hymn to Pan, Hesiod, the Homeric Hymns, and Homerica
s: is_a song [a song seeking Pan’s favour] The Pan hymn praises Pan’s appearance, roaming, hunting, music, dancing, and parentage. It recounts his birth to Hermes and the daughter of Dryops, his reception among the immortals, and the reason for his name. It closes with a greeting to Pan and a promise to remember him in another song.

l: Margites, Hesiod, the Homeric Hymns, and Homerica
s: A burlesque poem attributed to Homer, though Suidas names Pigres, using mixed metre and fragments portraying foolish Margites and a fox-hedgehog proverb.

l: Pigres, Hesiod, the Homeric Hymns, and Homerica
s: Pigres, a Carian from Halicarnassus and Artemisia’s brother, is identified by Suidas as author of Margites and Battle of the Frogs and Mice.

l: Trojan War, Hesiod, the Homeric Hymns, and Homerica
s: The Trojan War, planned by Zeus with Themis to reduce excessive human population, begins with the goddesses’ dispute and Alexandrus’s choice of Aphrodite. It proceeds through the Achaeans’ gathering and fighting around Troy. Believing it ended after dedicating the wooden horse, the Trojans feast; the Greeks attack and sack Ilium, followed by heroes’ returns.

l: Heroic Age, Hesiod, the Homeric Hymns, and Homerica
s: ends_with Telegony [with the end of the Cycle] The Heroic Age ended with the conclusion of the Cycle and the death of Odysseus. The Cycle therefore brought the Greek epic history of the world down to the end of the heroic period.

l: Homeric Hymns manuscript tradition, Hesiod, the Homeric Hymns, and Homerica
s: has_common_parent common parent [according to T. W. Allen] The Homeric Hymns manuscript tradition is represented by numerous medieval manuscripts enumerated by T. W. Allen. The manuscripts are traced to a common parent, from which three main families are derived, while M has a separate descent.

l: Demetrius Chalcondyles, Hesiod, the Homeric Hymns, and Homerica
s: published Works and Days [Milan, editio princeps, containing only the Works and Days] Demetrius Chalcondyles produced an editio princeps of the Works and Days at Milan in 1493, or possibly 1493, and an edition of the Homeric Hymns at Florence in 1488. The latter also included the Epigrams and Battle of the Frogs and Mice.

l: Oxyrhynchus Papyri, Hesiod, the Homeric Hymns, and Homerica
s: The Oxyrhynchus Papyri provide witnesses for the Works and Days, Theogony, Shield of Heracles, and lost Hesiodic works. The unit specifically lists Oxyrhynchus Papyri 1090, 873, 689, 421, and 1358-9.

l: Hesiod manuscript tradition, Hesiod, the Homeric Hymns, and Homerica
s: The Hesiod manuscript tradition includes papyri and medieval manuscripts for the Works and Days, Theogony, and Shield of Heracles. The recovery of Hesiodic papyri generally confirms the authority of the medieval manuscripts while also supplying new lines and improved readings.

l: Works and Days manuscripts, Hesiod, the Homeric Hymns, and Homerica
s: The Works and Days manuscripts comprise S and A–Q, including an Oxyrhynchus Papyri witness, spanning the fourth to fifteenth centuries and grouped by Rudolf Rzach into six families.

l: Theogony manuscripts, Hesiod, the Homeric Hymns, and Homerica
s: Theogony manuscripts are papyri and medieval codices designated N, O, A–I, and K–L, unfolding into families Ωa (C,D), Ωb (E,F), Ωc (G,H,I), and Ψ (K,L).

l: Shield of Heracles manuscripts, Hesiod, the Homeric Hymns, and Homerica
s: The Shield of Heracles manuscripts comprise papyrus and medieval witnesses, chiefly organized into Ωa, Ωb, Ψa, and Ψb families, ending with N and O identified as mixed-family manuscripts.

l: Homeric Hymns manuscript families, Hesiod, the Homeric Hymns, and Homerica
s: Homeric Hymns manuscript families comprise x1, x2, y, and p, derived from a common parent; x1 and x2 list their members, p has many, while M is excluded for separate descent.

l: Aldine edition, Hesiod, the Homeric Hymns, and Homerica
s: contains complete works [of Hesiod] The Aldine edition of Hesiod was published at Venice in 1495 and contained the complete works. The Aldine edition of the Homeric Hymns was published at Venice in 1504.

l: Rzach editions of Hesiod, Hesiod, the Homeric Hymns, and Homerica
s: include 1902 larger edition and 1913 smaller edition [Leipzig] Rzach’s editions of Hesiod include a larger Leipzig edition of 1902 and a smaller edition of 1913. The unit identifies these editions as important resources for Hesiodic poems and fragments.

l: Allen and Sikes edition, Hesiod, the Homeric Hymns, and Homerica
s: The 1904 London edition of Homeric Hymns is valued throughout for its conjecture-purged text, introduction, and notes.

l: Greek literature, Hesiod, the Homeric Hymns, and Homerica
s: The unit recommends the ordinary histories of Greek literature for the Hesiodic poems, especially the work of Croiset. It also notes that the summary account in Prof. Murray’s Ancient Greek Literature has a strong sceptical bias.

l: papyrus fragments, Hesiod, the Homeric Hymns, and Homerica
s: confirm medieval manuscripts [in general] Papyrus fragments confirm much of the authority of the medieval manuscripts and provide new lines, improved readings, and fragments of lost works. The most numerous and valuable discoveries concern the Catalogues.

l: medieval manuscripts, Hesiod, the Homeric Hymns, and Homerica
s: Medieval manuscripts preserve the principal textual traditions of Hesiod and the Homeric Hymns. For Hesiod, papyrus discoveries generally confirm their authority; for the Homeric Hymns, T. W. Allen traces the listed medieval manuscripts to a common parent.

l: Strife, Hesiod, the Homeric Hymns, and Homerica
s: Strife is a goddess of two kinds: a blameworthy form fostering cruel war and battle, and a wholesome form promoting work by driving neighbours, craftsmen, beggars, and minstrels to compete for wealth. At Peleus and Thetis’s marriage feast, she begins the dispute over whether Hera, Athena, or Aphrodite is fairest.

l: Night, Hesiod, the Homeric Hymns, and Homerica
s: Night, primordial goddess, arose from Chaos, bore Aether and Day with Erebus, then without anyone bore Doom, Fate, Death, Sleep, Dreams, Blame, Woe, and Strife.

l: Demeter, Hesiod, the Homeric Hymns, and Homerica
s: Demeter is a deathless, rich-haired, awful goddess, daughter of Rhea and mother of Persephone, who provides holy grain and holds honour among gods and mortals. After Hades abducts Persephone, she searches with flaming torches, refusing ambrosia, nectar, food, drink, and red wine. Disguised as the old woman Doso, she enters Celeus’ household, nurses Demophoon, and reveals herself after Metaneira interrupts her effort to make him immortal. She orders a temple and altar at Eleusis, then withdraws, hides the seed, and causes famine until Persephone returns. She restores the earth’s fertility, teaches the Eleusinian Mysteries and rites to human rulers, and is invoked with Zeus of the Earth for sound, heavy grain and the city’s safety.

l: Iapetus, Hesiod, the Homeric Hymns, and Homerica
s: is_parent_of Prometheus [through Clymene] Iapetus takes Clymene, daughter of Ocean, as his wife and fathers Atlas, Menoetius, Prometheus, and Epimetheus.

l: fire, Hesiod, the Homeric Hymns, and Homerica
s: Fire is an unwearying, far-seen gleam Zeus hides from mortal men after Prometheus’s deception. Prometheus steals it in a hollow fennel stalk for men’s use. Zeus calls it a great plague to Prometheus and men and creates Pandora as the price.

l: Hephaestus, Hesiod, the Homeric Hymns, and Homerica
s: Hephaestus is a craftsman and famed worker, more skilled in crafts than all the sons of Heaven. He is famed for inventions, teaches men glorious gifts and crafts with Athene, and is husband of Aglaea. He gives Cedalion to guide Orion and, at Zeus’s command, makes Heracles’ armor and an intricate shield.

l: gods, Hesiod, the Homeric Hymns, and Homerica
s: The gods are immortal, deathless beings who govern both their own divine order and important aspects of mortal life. They create the races of mortal men, hide the means of life, ordain labor, and make sweat the path between men and Goodness. Mortals must pray, keep ritual purity, honor the gods, observe sacred days and bird omens, and offer sacrifices; violations bring trouble. Hecate holds exceptional honor among the deathless gods and shares in earth, heaven, and sea. After a ten-year struggle with the Titans, aided by Cottus, Gyes, and Briareos, the gods settle the contest for honors by force, press Olympian Zeus to rule, and receive divided dignities. Their order is upheld by Styx oaths, whose perjurers suffer breathlessness and exclusion. They may also be divided by strife, as when Zeus considers separating them from mortals. They gather on Olympus for judgments, including that of Hermes and Apollo, and in heaven watch the battle of Frogs and Mice before Zeus sends aid to the Frogs.

l: men, Hesiod, the Homeric Hymns, and Homerica
s: Men are mortal people whose lives depend on work, justice, the gods, and the earth. Formerly they dwelled in mountain caves and resembled wild beasts; through Hephaestus they learned crafts and came to live peacefully in their own houses throughout the year. They receive fire after Prometheus steals it from Zeus, burn white bones to the deathless gods, and lay up offerings in Nysa’s shrines, yet they lack a seer who knows Zeus’s mind. Zeus gives them right unlike beasts and birds, judging justice and violence, while their lot includes toil, sickness, sorrow, marriage, poverty, and death. They must plough, sow, harvest, make tools, store grain, and heed seasonal signs, since idleness brings hunger. Demeter’s anger causes famine and threatens their destruction and their gifts to the gods; through her they receive the Eleusinian Mysteries. Earth can bless them with children, harvests, wealth, cattle, and orderly cities.

l: golden race, Hesiod, the Homeric Hymns, and Homerica
s: The golden race lives under Cronos without sorrow, toil, grief, or old age, receives effortless food, and after death becomes kindly guardians who give wealth.

l: Silver Race, Hesiod, the Homeric Hymns, and Homerica
s: The Silver Race is a second mortal generation, less noble than the golden race. Some attribute it to Earth, and Hesiod’s Great Works makes it part of Earth’s family. It remains childish for a hundred years, becomes foolish and violent, fails to honor the gods, and Zeus destroys it.

l: brazen race, Hesiod, the Homeric Hymns, and Homerica
s: The brazen race, a third mortal generation sprung from ash-trees, is strong, violent, war-loving, bronze-using, and ultimately destroys itself.

l: race of mortal men half-divine, Hesiod, the Homeric Hymns, and Homerica
s: The race of heroes is a fourth generation of half-divine mortal men, nobler and more righteous than the brazen race; war destroys some, while Zeus grants others sorrow-free dwelling in the Islands of the Blessed.

l: Troy, Hesiod, the Homeric Hymns, and Homerica
s: Troy is a closely besieged city of the Trojans. Alexandrus and Helen arrive there after fleeing Sparta, while Aeneas is foretold to reign among its people. Greeks attack its surroundings and defenders; after Alexandrus dies, the inhabitants alter their wall, bring in a wooden horse, celebrate apparent victory, and Troy is captured.

l: Helen, Hesiod, the Homeric Hymns, and Homerica
s: Helen is a woman whose origins differ across accounts: Hesiod makes her daughter of Ocean and Zeus, while other records link her birth to Zeus, Tyndareus, or Nemesis. Described as an Argive maiden with Aphrodite’s beauty, she is sought by many heroes and becomes Menelaus’s wife after an oath among her suitors; she bears Hermione and Nicostratus. While Menelaus is away, Aphrodite promises her to Alexandrus, and she leaves Sparta with him for Ilium, dishonouring Menelaus. At Ilium she recognizes the disguised Odysseus and helps plan the city’s capture. After Alexandrus dies, she marries Deiphobus and consents to Aethra’s release. When Ilium falls, Menelaus recognizes and takes her to the ships.

l: Justice, Hesiod, the Homeric Hymns, and Homerica
s: Justice, Zeus’s honored virgin daughter, reports human wrongdoing, leaves cities that reject her, prospers those with straight judgements, protects cities, and eventually defeats Outrage.

l: princes, Hesiod, the Homeric Hymns, and Homerica
s: give judgement [justly or crookedly] Princes are warned that the gods watch them and that whole cities may suffer for their crooked judgements. They are told to make their judgements straight and reject bribes.

l: city, Hesiod, the Homeric Hymns, and Homerica
s: flourishes prosperity [when its rulers give straight judgements] A city that gives straight judgements flourishes, while one ruled by violence and crooked judgement suffers famine, plague, war, and destruction. Justice and Peace support the prosperous city.

l: violence, Hesiod, the Homeric Hymns, and Homerica
s: is bad [for poor and prosperous alike] Violence is condemned as harmful to both poor and prosperous men. Zeus punishes those who practice it, while Justice eventually defeats Outrage.

l: work, Hesiod, the Homeric Hymns, and Homerica
s: Work is presented as honorable and necessary, improving every person’s lot by producing wealth. Sustained, properly ordered labor fills barns, protects against hunger, and wins divine favor; more hands and work bring more increase, while promised wages should be fixed.

l: hunger, Hesiod, the Homeric Hymns, and Homerica
s: accompanies sluggard [as a fitting companion] Hunger is described as the fitting companion of the sluggard. Work keeps hunger away, while idleness leaves a person in need.

l: wealth, Hesiod, the Homeric Hymns, and Homerica
s: Wealth is desired as a motive for labor. It is best when god-given and honestly increased, not gained through violence, theft, or deceit, since wrongful wealth is temporary. Through fixed wages, work upon work, and an only son, it increases and preserves a father’s house.

l: inheritance dispute, Hesiod, the Homeric Hymns, and Homerica
s: is_settled_by judgement [true and fair] The inheritance dispute concerns Perses taking a greater share and bribing or influencing lords who judge the case. Hesiod urges that the dispute be settled with true judgement and warns that Perses must not repeat such conduct.

l: judgement, Hesiod, the Homeric Hymns, and Homerica
s: Judgement must be straight, truthful, and free from bribes. Crooked judgement harms the city and brings punishment from Zeus, while fair judgement brings peace and prosperity.

l: war, Hesiod, the Homeric Hymns, and Homerica
s: destroys race of heroes [in part, through battle] War is associated with the harmful form of Strife, violence, and the destruction of mortal races. It destroys parts of the race of heroes and may be sent by Zeus against unjust cities.

l: Pandora's creation, Hesiod, the Homeric Hymns, and Homerica
s: Pandora’s creation is a sheer, hopeless snare devised by Zeus after Prometheus steals fire. Zeus commands the Limping God to form a maiden from earth and water; Athene and other gods adorn her with clothing, beauty, speech, and deceptive qualities, making her irresistible guile.

l: trust, Hesiod, the Homeric Hymns, and Homerica
s: ruins men [alike with mistrust] Trust, like mistrust, ruins men. A promised wage should be fixed and witnessed even when it concerns a friend or brother.

l: mistrust, Hesiod, the Homeric Hymns, and Homerica
s: ruins men [alike with trust] Mistrust, like trust, ruins men. A witness should be obtained when fixing a promised wage.

l: flaunting woman, Hesiod, the Homeric Hymns, and Homerica
s: A flaunting woman coaxes, cozens, and deceives a man while seeking his barn.

l: womankind, Hesiod, the Homeric Hymns, and Homerica
s: is_trusted_as deceivers [by a man who trusts them] Womankind is described as deceptive to the man who trusts it.

l: only son, Hesiod, the Homeric Hymns, and Homerica
s: The sole son feeds his father’s house, increasing the home’s wealth.

l: second son, Hesiod, the Homeric Hymns, and Homerica
s: If a man leaves a second son, he should die old.

l: Dionysus, Hesiod, the Homeric Hymns, and Homerica
s: Dionysus is a heaven-born, immortal god, son of Semele and Zeus, also called Insewn and inspirer of frenzied women. Born from Semele through union with Zeus at remote Nysa, he is fostered carefully by Nymphs in a sweet-smelling cave and grows into their ivy- and laurel-wreathed leader, wandering continually through woody coombes. He provides joyful wine from the grape harvest, is god of abundant clusters, receives perfect sacrificial hecatombs at feasts every three years, and is sung at the beginning and end of a strain. Appearing as a young man on a sea headland, he is captured by pirates, displays signs aboard their ship, becomes a lion, punishes them, and spares the helmsman. He makes Ariadne deathless and unageing for him.

l: Sirius, Hesiod, the Homeric Hymns, and Homerica
s: Sirius is a star associated with oppressive summer heat: it briefly passes over men by day as autumn nears, then parches heads and knees and dries skin in intense heat.

l: Orion, Hesiod, the Homeric Hymns, and Homerica
s: Orion, son of Euryale and Poseidon, had rude strength and could walk on waves. He outraged Merope at Chios while drunk, was blinded by Oenopion, guided east by Cedalion, and healed by Sun. He piled up Peloris, founded the close of Poseidon, and settled in Euboea. Hunting with Artemis and Leto in Crete, he was killed by Earth’s scorpion, died from its sting, and Zeus placed him among the stars.

l: Hellenes, Hesiod, the Homeric Hymns, and Homerica
s: The Hellenes admired Homer’s answers and called some of his verses golden. They favored Homer after hearing the finest passages from both poets, but Paneides overruled them and awarded the victory to Hesiod.

l: the slaves, Hesiod, the Homeric Hymns, and Homerica
s: winnow grain [after Orion first appears] Slaves are assigned agricultural and household work, including following the oxen, scattering seed, hiding seed from birds, harvesting, winnowing grain, and carrying out commands. They are to work in wet and dry conditions during the ploughing season, and in midsummer they are told to build barns.

l: oxen, Hesiod, the Homeric Hymns, and Homerica
s: Two nine-year-old oxen, best for agricultural labor and seasonal work, are chosen for ploughing; vulnerable to fighting in the furrow, they are fed, winter-rationed, and rested after work.

l: agricultural labor and seasonal work, Hesiod, the Homeric Hymns, and Homerica
s: Agricultural labor and seasonal work is a cycle governed by seasonal signs and calendar guidance. It demands timely effort, weather-appropriate clothing, oxen for ploughing, and early rising at harvest, rewarding industry. Across the year it directs ploughing, sowing, pruning, harvesting, winnowing, storage, timber-cutting, vine and animal care, shearing, wine-opening, and work on ships when sailing is unsafe.

l: debts and hunger, Hesiod, the Homeric Hymns, and Homerica
s: threaten Perses [when he neglects work] Perses is warned to find a way to pay his debts and avoid hunger. If he delays work and must seek help from neighbors, they may refuse him after he has asked repeatedly.

l: house, Hesiod, the Homeric Hymns, and Homerica
s: is_required_for agricultural labor and seasonal work [as an initial provision] A house is listed among the first necessities, together with a woman and an ox for the plough. It should be prepared with supplies and barns so that work will not depend on another person’s assistance.

l: the plough, Hesiod, the Homeric Hymns, and Homerica
s: The plough is prepared at home in two forms, one-piece and jointed, so one replaces the other if it breaks; its parts are made from suitable woods including holm-oak.

l: grain and crops, Hesiod, the Homeric Hymns, and Homerica
s: Demeter’s holy grain is sown in ready soil, guarded from birds, becomes full corn-ears with Zeus’s good result, then is winnowed, measured, jarred, and kept indoors.

l: harvest, Hesiod, the Homeric Hymns, and Homerica
s: Harvest begins when the Pleiades rise: sharpen the sickle, rise early and bring fruits home, then cut grape-clusters, dry and cover them, and draw off wine.

l: winter, Hesiod, the Homeric Hymns, and Homerica
s: Winter follows autumn rains after heat abates, bringing frost, cold winds, snow, rain, and difficult conditions; before dark clouds arrive, prepare warm clothing, shelter, barns, and fodder, feeding men more food and oxen half.

l: spring, Hesiod, the Homeric Hymns, and Homerica
s: Spring is a grey seasonal marker that returns after winter, signaled by Arcturus, the swallow, and rising Pleiades; Earth bears varied fruit and fallow land may be ploughed.

l: rain, Hesiod, the Homeric Hymns, and Homerica
s: protects fallow land [when sufficient for late ploughing] Autumn rain makes men’s bodies feel easier and marks a season for cutting timber. Rain can also rescue late ploughing if Zeus sends it on the third day and it reaches the proper depth without exceeding an ox’s hoof.

l: Aulis, Hesiod, the Homeric Hymns, and Homerica
s: Aulis is where the Greek leaders first meet and sacrifice before the expedition. The forces later muster there a second time, but stormy winds sent by Artemis prevent them from sailing.

l: Achaeans, Hesiod, the Homeric Hymns, and Homerica
s: The Achaeans assemble at Aulis for sacrifice, witness signs and prophecy, then attack Ilium, demand Helen and treasure, and ravage nearby cities. After Achilles’ death, they contest Thersites’ killing, honour Achilles and Antilochus with burial rites and games, and dispute Achilles’ arms. They besiege Ilium, use a wooden horse, return from Tenedos after Sinon’s fire-signal, storm the city, kill or capture inhabitants, divide spoils, and sail away.

l: Leto, Hesiod, the Homeric Hymns, and Homerica
s: Leto is a queenly, divine goddess, daughter of Coeus and rich-haired mother of Artemis and Apollo. After traveling many lands, she secures Delos, endures nine days and nights of labor, and gives birth to Apollo beside a palm tree. She later remains beside him in Zeus’s house, tending his bow and quiver.

l: sea, Hesiod, the Homeric Hymns, and Homerica
s: The sea is a fruitless, deep natural feature ruled and moved by Poseidon. It is harmless during the steady-wind sailing season and passable in spring, but becomes dangerous with autumn storms; ignorant or overloaded sailors risk death.

l: sea-faring and sailing, Hesiod, the Homeric Hymns, and Homerica
s: Sea-faring is a livelihood when poverty leaves insufficient livelihood. It should be avoided as the Pleiades descend and winter gales begin; its favourable season comes fifty days after the solstice, while spring sailing is risky, and sailors must return before new wine, autumn rain, and storms of Notus.

l: the ship, Hesiod, the Homeric Hymns, and Homerica
s: A swift, many-thwarted sea-going ship carries trade and profit when suitably loaded. If sea-faring is desired, it is readied with tackle, wings, rudder, and measured cargo; otherwise it is hauled ashore, drained, protected, and its equipment stored.

l: destructive winds, Hesiod, the Homeric Hymns, and Homerica
s: Gales of many kinds rage when the Pleiades plunge into the sea or escape Orion’s strength. Notus accompanies Zeus’s heavy autumn rain, stirs and endangers the sea, though winds become steady and favorable fifty days after the solstice. Winds from Typhoeus bring havoc: they scatter ships, destroy sailors, and fill fields with dust and cruel uproar, spoiling them.

l: riches and wealth, Hesiod, the Homeric Hymns, and Homerica
s: Riches and wealth provide life to poor mortals and follow the blessed man. Hecate bestows them on those whose prayers she favorably receives. In sea-trading, greater cargo can increase wealth if winds prevent harmful gales, but carrying too much endangers it through disaster at sea; one should not risk all goods.

l: marriage and household, Hesiod, the Homeric Hymns, and Homerica
s: Marriage is presented as a household choice to make near age thirty. A man should choose a nearby grown maiden, marry her so he can teach her careful ways, and value a good wife as the greatest household gain, while avoiding a bad, greedy wife who brings misery and old age.

l: friendship and social conduct, Hesiod, the Homeric Hymns, and Homerica
s: Friendship and social conduct require treating friends justly, though not exactly as brothers, and repaying unreconciled wrongs doubly. The guidance then urges avoidance of shifting friendships, lavishness, churlishness, rogues, slander, boasting, taunting the poor, boorish feasting, and harmful speech.

l: ritual purity and religious observance, Hesiod, the Homeric Hymns, and Homerica
s: A topic of ritual purity and religious observance: washed hands and prayer are required before libations and river crossings, while pollution, mockery, and other impure acts are forbidden. It expands from water rites to cleanliness, burial, childbirth, exposure, urination, plant-cutting, and divine punishment.

l: the calendar and auspicious days, Hesiod, the Homeric Hymns, and Homerica
s: The calendar and auspicious days comes from Zeus and marks days for observance. It unfolds by assigning monthly dates to work review, supplies, holy observances, travel, planting, births, marriage, animal work, ships, jars, and yoking; the fifth and some other days are unfavourable or changeable. The thirtieth is best for reviewing work and distributing supplies.

l: The Divination by Birds, Hesiod, the Homeric Hymns, and Homerica
s: The Divination by Birds is placed by some after verse 828 of Works and Days. Apollonius of Rhodes rejects it as spurious.

l: Maia, Hesiod, the Homeric Hymns, and Homerica
s: Maia is a rich-tressed, shy nymph and goddess, daughter of Atlas, who avoids the deathless gods and lives in a deep shadowy cave on Cyllene. Zeus visits her there at night; she bears Hermes on the fourth day of the month, then rebukes him when he returns at night, warning that Apollo may punish his actions.

l: Hyades, Hesiod, the Homeric Hymns, and Homerica
s: The Hyades are stars identified as transformed sisters of Hyas, named Phaesyle, Coronis, Cleeia, Phaco, and Eudora.

l: Coronis, Hesiod, the Homeric Hymns, and Homerica
s: is_daughter_of King Phlegyas Coronis is the daughter of King Phlegyas. She bore Asclepius in the Dotian plain.

l: Great Bear, Hesiod, the Homeric Hymns, and Homerica
s: The Great Bear is Callisto, placed among the stars by Zeus and named Bear because of her misfortune.

l: Callisto, Hesiod, the Homeric Hymns, and Homerica
s: Callisto, Lycaon’s daughter in Arcadia, hunted with Artemis among wild beasts. After Zeus seduced her and Artemis discovered her pregnancy, Artemis transformed her into a bear; she gave birth to Arcas and Zeus placed her among the stars.

l: Lycaon, Hesiod, the Homeric Hymns, and Homerica
s: Callisto’s father receives her and her babe, entertains Zeus while feigning ignorance, and serves the cut-up babe at his banquet.

l: Arcas, Hesiod, the Homeric Hymns, and Homerica
s: Arcas, son of Callisto and Zeus, lives in Lycaeum, was given with his mother to Lycaon, pursued her, and is identified as Bootes, Bear-warden.

l: Oenopion, Hesiod, the Homeric Hymns, and Homerica
s: blinds Orion [in punishment for Orion’s outrage against Merope] Oenopion was the father of Merope. After Orion outraged Merope while drunk, Oenopion had Orion blinded and expelled from the country, and later hid underground when Orion returned seeking punishment.

l: Chios, Hesiod, the Homeric Hymns, and Homerica
s: Rocky island Chios is home of a blind singer, claimed as Homer, whose songs are declared supreme and sweetest by the poet-narrator.

l: Crete, Hesiod, the Homeric Hymns, and Homerica
s: Crete was settled by Pelasgi, Achaeans, and Dorians, the Three-fold People, who divided the land into three parts.

l: scorpion, Hesiod, the Homeric Hymns, and Homerica
s: A very large creature sent by Earth after Orion threatened to kill every beast, it stung and killed him; Zeus placed it among the stars as a memorial.

l: Orion’s transformation into a constellation, Hesiod, the Homeric Hymns, and Homerica
s: After Orion was killed by the scorpion, Zeus placed him among the stars at the request of Artemis and Leto because of his manliness. Hesiod also says that Orion was taken into the number of the stars after settling in Euboea.

l: Orion and the scorpion among the stars, Hesiod, the Homeric Hymns, and Homerica
s: Zeus placed both Orion and the scorpion among the stars. The scorpion was set there as a memorial of Orion and of the events that led to his death.

l: Cyllene, Hesiod, the Homeric Hymns, and Homerica
s: contains Hermes [Hermes has a sacred place there as its god] Cyllene is identified as Hermes's domain and as the forest-clad mountain containing Maia's deep-shadowed cave. Hermes is born there and returns there after stealing Apollo's cattle.

l: Arcadia, Hesiod, the Homeric Hymns, and Homerica
s: Arcadia, a land of many springs and flocks, contains Hermes’s sacred place; there he tended sheep, desired Dryops’s daughter, and fathered Pan.

l: Orion’s death, Hesiod, the Homeric Hymns, and Homerica
s: Orion died after Earth sent a very large scorpion against him because he threatened to kill every beast on earth. The scorpion stung him, after which Zeus placed Orion among the stars.

l: The Precepts of Chiron, Hesiod, the Homeric Hymns, and Homerica
s: A book of precepts teaches sacrifices to eternal gods on returning home and hearing both sides before judgment, includes advice on educating children and a lifespan comparison, and ends with disputed attribution: once Hesiod’s, rejected by Aristophanes.

l: rich-haired Nymphs, Hesiod, the Homeric Hymns, and Homerica
s: Rich-haired Nymphs, goddesses and daughters of Zeus, receive, foster, and raise Dionysus in Nysa’s dells, then follow him through wooded valleys, filling the forest with outcry.

l: Aristophanes, Hesiod, the Homeric Hymns, and Homerica
s: A critic, Aristophanes is identified as the first to reject The Precepts of Chiron as a work of Hesiod.

l: Great Works, Hesiod, the Homeric Hymns, and Homerica
s: The Great Works is a work containing verse on Rhadamanthys' slaying, evil's increased harvest, reciprocal justice, and silver as part of Earth's family.

l: Idaean Dactyls, Hesiod, the Homeric Hymns, and Homerica
s: The Idaean Dactyls, located in Crete, were said by Hesiod to teach iron smelting and tempering, beginning with Celmis and Damnameneus.

l: Cyprus, Hesiod, the Homeric Hymns, and Homerica
s: Cyprus is a sea-girt, sea-set island and Aphrodite’s sweet-smelling home, birthplace, and dominion. Its walled cities include Paphos, with her precinct, temple, and fragrant altar. She arrives there over the sea in soft foam, prepares in rich clothing, then travels toward Troy and Mount Ida.

l: Celmis, Hesiod, the Homeric Hymns, and Homerica
s: Celmis, one of the first Idaean Dactyls, is said to have discovered iron in Cyprus.

l: Damnameneus, Hesiod, the Homeric Hymns, and Homerica
s: Damnameneus, one of the first Idaean Dactyls, is said by Clement to have discovered iron in Cyprus.

l: Delas, Hesiod, the Homeric Hymns, and Homerica
s: Delas, an Idaean Dactyl also called Scythes by Hesiod, is identified as discovering bronze smelting.

l: Scythes, Hesiod, the Homeric Hymns, and Homerica
s: Scythes is the name Hesiod gives to Delas.

l: iron, Hesiod, the Homeric Hymns, and Homerica
s: is_located_in Cyprus [as the site of its discovery] Iron was discovered in Cyprus by Celmis and Damnameneus, according to Clement. Hesiod says that the Idaean Dactyls taught its smelting and tempering in Crete.

l: bronze, Hesiod, the Homeric Hymns, and Homerica
s: Bronze smelting was discovered by Delas, according to Clement.

l: tempering of iron, Hesiod, the Homeric Hymns, and Homerica
s: Hesiod says that the Idaean Dactyls taught the tempering of iron in Crete.

l: discovery of iron, Hesiod, the Homeric Hymns, and Homerica
s: The discovery of iron in Cyprus is attributed by Clement to Celmis and Damnameneus, the first Idaean Dactyls.

l: bronze smelting, Hesiod, the Homeric Hymns, and Homerica
s: Bronze smelting was discovered by Delas, whom Hesiod calls Scythes.

l: Hera, Hesiod, the Homeric Hymns, and Homerica
s: Hera is a golden-throned, beautiful queen of the immortals, born to Rhea and Cronos, sister and wife of Zeus, and reverenced and honoured by the blessed on high Olympus. As Zeus’s blooming wife, she bears Hebe, Ares, and Eileithyia; during anger and quarrel with him, she bears Hephaestus without union. Her conflicts shape much of the record: she and Zeus choose Teiresias to judge pleasure in intercourse, and she blinds him in anger at his answer. After discovering Zeus’s seduction of her priestess Io, she has Argus watch Io after Zeus changes her into a white cow. Angry when Zeus gives birth to Athena without her, she seeks a child without Zeus and gives Typhaon to the dragoness. She also contests beauty with Athena and Aphrodite, then sends a storm against Alexandrus and Helen.

l: Selene, Hesiod, the Homeric Hymns, and Homerica
s: Selene is a white-armed, bright, mild, bright-tressed goddess, child of Hyperion and Euryphaessa and daughter of Pallas. Radiant beneath a golden crown, she drives her long-maned horses in a mid-month orbit, her increasing light a sure sign to mortals. At eventime she bathes in Ocean, harnesses her team, and, after joining Zeus in love, bears Pandia.

l: Oceanus, Hesiod, the Homeric Hymns, and Homerica
s: Oceanus, a Titan born from Earth and Heaven, with Tethys fathers rivers and many daughters serving earth and deep waters.

l: Olympus, Hesiod, the Homeric Hymns, and Homerica
s: Olympus is a high, glorious, snowy home and dwelling place of Zeus, the Muses, and the undying gods. The Muses sing there, and its snowy heights hold assemblies of the immortals, Zeus’s scales of judgment, and the gods’ oaths by Styx. Zeus calls the deathless gods there before fighting the Titans, comes from it hurling lightning, and it reels during that battle. Styx first arrives there with her children in support of Zeus. Hermes and Apollo reach it after their dispute; Heracles lives there happily after his works. Finally, it reels horribly when Pallas Athene springs from Zeus’s head armed for war.

l: Pieria, Hesiod, the Homeric Hymns, and Homerica
s: Pieria is the place where Apollo's divine cattle are kept and graze in pleasant meadows. Hermes goes there at night, cuts fifty cattle from the herd, and drives them away.

l: Mnemosyne, Hesiod, the Homeric Hymns, and Homerica
s: Mnemosyne, Titaness and goddess of memory, reigns over Eleuther's hills; after nine nights with Zeus, she bears nine Muses whose songs ease sorrow and ills.

l: Eros, Hesiod, the Homeric Hymns, and Homerica
s: Eros, an early-born and fairest deathless god rising from Ocean, overcomes gods and men through desire, unnerving limbs and minds.

l: Erebus, Hesiod, the Homeric Hymns, and Homerica
s: is_a underworld region [misty and gloomy] Erebus is the dark region from which Hermes is commanded to bring Persephone back to the gods. Persephone is described as returning from Erebus to the light after Hermes reaches Hades’s house.

l: Cottus, Hesiod, the Homeric Hymns, and Homerica
s: Cottus, a deathless god with a hundred arms, is bound beneath the earth by his father for his great strength and size. Restored by Zeus and the gods, he pledges aid and hurls three hundred rocks against the Titans.

l: Briareos, Hesiod, the Homeric Hymns, and Homerica
s: is_son_in_law_of Poseidon [Poseidon gave him Cymopolea to wed] Briareos is brought back from bondage beneath the earth and fights the Titans with Cottus and Gyes. He later dwells on Ocean's foundations, and the Earth-Shaker makes him his son-in-law by giving him Cymopolea.

l: Gyes, Hesiod, the Homeric Hymns, and Homerica
s: has one hundred arms [springing from his shoulders] Gyes is one of the mighty beings imprisoned beneath the earth by his father. After being released, he fights the Titans with Cottus and Briareos and later lives in Tartarus as a trusted warder of Zeus.

l: Aphrodite's birth, Hesiod, the Homeric Hymns, and Homerica
s: is_a divine birth [foam-born origin of Aphrodite] After Cronos cut off Heaven's members and cast them into the sea, foam formed around the immortal flesh and a maiden grew within it. She approached Cythera and then Cyprus, where she emerged as Aphrodite.

l: Medusa, Hesiod, the Homeric Hymns, and Homerica
s: Medusa was one of the Gorgons born to Ceto and Phorcys and was mortal, unlike her two sisters. After Perseus cut off her head, Chrysaor and Pegasus sprang from her.

l: Sphinx, Hesiod, the Homeric Hymns, and Homerica
s: killed Haemon The Sphinx killed Haemon, the son of Creon.

l: Iolaus, Hesiod, the Homeric Hymns, and Homerica
s: Iolaus, son of Iphiclus and companion of Heracles, drives Arion and serves as charioteer and fellow warrior, preparing to confront Cycnus and Ares.

l: Alpheus, Hesiod, the Homeric Hymns, and Homerica
s: Alpheus is the river to which Hermes drives Apollo's cattle before dawn. Hermes throws his sandals into its deep-eddying water and quenches the fire's embers there.

l: Styx, Hesiod, the Homeric Hymns, and Homerica
s: Styx is an Oceanid and goddess, chiefest and eldest daughter of Ocean and Tethys. With Pallas she bore four children, first supported Zeus against the Titans, then dwelt with Zeus as the gods’ great oath.

l: divine song, Hesiod, the Homeric Hymns, and Homerica
s: is_a song [inspired by the Muses] Divine song is taught by the Muses and celebrates things that were, are, and will be. It honors gods and ancient men, gives princes persuasive speech, and relieves sorrow when a singer chants the glorious deeds of the past.

l: divine genealogy, Hesiod, the Homeric Hymns, and Homerica
s: describes gods [origins and lineage] The divine genealogy traces the immortals from Chaos, Earth, Tartarus, and Eros through the births of the Titans, Olympians, rivers, goddesses, and monsters. It also records how the gods divided honors and how Zeus came to rule.

l: sickle, Hesiod, the Homeric Hymns, and Homerica
s: Earth made a great sickle from grey flint and placed it in Cronos's hands. Cronos used the jagged sickle to cut off Heaven's members during an ambush.

l: thunderbolt, Hesiod, the Homeric Hymns, and Homerica
s: Given to Zeus by released sons of Heaven after he releases them, the thunderbolt becomes his formidable weapon. He uses its fire, heat, and noise to overwhelm the Titans' armies, then casts it at Hera's urging, frightening Frogs and Mice without ending the Mice's hope.

l: Hecate, Hesiod, the Homeric Hymns, and Homerica
s: Hecate is a goddess, born to Phoebe and Coeus, though also recorded as daughter of Persaeus. Zeus honours her above all, gives her splendid gifts and shares in earth and the unfruitful sea, while the deathless gods honour her in heaven. She keeps privileges in earth, heaven, and sea from the first division among the former Titan gods. By her will she aids and advances people, influences judgment, assemblies, battle, games, horsemen, sea catches, and livestock, and Zeus appoints her nurse of the young. Later, she alone hears Persephone’s cries from her cave, tells Demeter what she heard, accompanies her to Helios, and becomes Persephone’s companion and minister.

l: earth, Hesiod, the Homeric Hymns, and Homerica
s: produces grain and crops [when Demeter restores fertility] The earth becomes barren when Demeter hides the seed, leaving fields without sprouting grain and the plain of Rharus leafless. After Demeter agrees to return, the earth produces leaves, flowers, and abundant grain.

l: division of Hecate's portion, Hesiod, the Homeric Hymns, and Homerica
s: is_established_at the beginning [at the first division] Hecate's portion was divided at the first from the beginning among earth, heaven, and sea. Zeus preserves all of this portion for her and takes nothing away.

l: sacrifices and prayers, Hesiod, the Homeric Hymns, and Homerica
s: invoke Hecate [according to custom; on earth] When people on earth offer rich sacrifices and pray according to custom, they call upon Hecate for favour. When she receives their prayers favourably, great honour and wealth come to them.

l: honour, Hesiod, the Homeric Hymns, and Homerica
s: is_received_by Hecate [from the deathless gods] Hecate receives honour in starry heaven and from the deathless gods, and Zeus honours her above all. She also gives honour and glory to those whom she chooses, including victors in battle and contests.

l: nursing of the young, Hesiod, the Homeric Hymns, and Homerica
s: is_role_of Hecate [from the beginning] Zeus makes Hecate a nurse of the young who, after that day, see the light of all-seeing Dawn. From the beginning, nursing the young is included among her honours.

l: Parnassus, Hesiod, the Homeric Hymns, and Homerica
s: Parnassus is the mountain beneath whose glades Apollo establishes his temple at Crisa. The Cretans follow Apollo to its ridge and reach the sanctuary where they are to dwell.

l: the underworld, Hesiod, the Homeric Hymns, and Homerica
s: The underworld is the hidden realm beneath the earth where Hades rules and Persephone is taken. Persephone must return there for one-third of every year after eating the pomegranate seed.

l: the birth and concealment of Zeus, Hesiod, the Homeric Hymns, and Homerica
s: occurs_in Crete Rhea asks Earth and Heaven to hide Zeus's birth from Cronos. Earth carries him to Crete, places him in a remote cave on Mount Aegeum, and leaves Cronos a stone wrapped in swaddling clothes.

l: the swallowing and regurgitation of Cronos's children, Hesiod, the Homeric Hymns, and Homerica
s: is_caused_by Zeus [through his arts and might] Cronos swallows Hestia, Demeter, Hera, Hades, the Earth-Shaker, and Zeus as they are born. After Zeus grows strong, Cronos is beguiled by Earth and vomits up the stone and then the children he had swallowed.

l: the release of the Cyclopes, Hesiod, the Homeric Hymns, and Homerica
s: concerns the thunderbolt [the Cyclopes gave it to Zeus afterward] Zeus sets free the brothers of his father, the sons of Heaven whom Cronos had bound. In gratitude, they give Zeus the thunder, the glowing thunderbolt, and lightning.

l: the division of the ox at Mecone, Hesiod, the Homeric Hymns, and Homerica
s: is_devised_by Prometheus [to deceive Zeus] At Mecone, Prometheus divides a great ox into portions for gods and mortal men. He hides the flesh under the paunch and covers the bones with fat, and Zeus's choice establishes the practice of burning white bones to the deathless gods.

l: the punishment of Prometheus, Hesiod, the Homeric Hymns, and Homerica
s: Zeus binds Prometheus with inextricable bonds and drives a shaft through his middle. A long-winged eagle eats his immortal liver each day, though it grows again at night, until Heracles kills the eagle and releases him with Zeus's consent.

l: the stone given to Cronos, Hesiod, the Homeric Hymns, and Homerica
s: is_substituted_for Zeus [as the child hidden from Cronos] Earth gives Cronos a great stone wrapped in swaddling clothes instead of the newborn Zeus. Cronos swallows it, and Zeus later sets it in the earth at Pytho as a sign and marvel to mortal men.

l: the imprisonment of the Titans, Hesiod, the Homeric Hymns, and Homerica
s: is_guarded_by Cottus [along with Gyes and Briareus] After their defeat, the Titans are buried beneath the wide-pathed earth and bound in bitter chains. They are confined in Tartarus behind bronze gates and walls under the watch of Gyes, Cottus, and Obriareus.

l: sea, Hesiod, the Homeric Hymns, and Homerica
s: The sea is a ruthless, white-surfaced, loud-moaning place, becoming still when the Dioscuri calm winds and waves.

l: winds (from Typhoeus), Hesiod, the Homeric Hymns, and Homerica
s: Boisterous winds come from Typhoeus after Zeus drives the Titans from heaven; Notus, Boreas, and clear Zephyr are excluded as god-sent blessings, while other winds blow fitfully.

l: Typhoeus's defeat, Hesiod, the Homeric Hymns, and Homerica
s: Zeus's defeat of Typhoeus involves thunder, lightning, fire, and a thunderbolt that burns the monster's heads. Typhoeus is hurled down as a maimed wreck and then cast into Tartarus.

l: Metis, Hesiod, the Homeric Hymns, and Homerica
s: Metis is Zeus’s first wife, a goddess called wisest among gods and mortal men, and Athene’s mother. When about to bear Athene and a son destined to rule, Zeus deceives and swallows her. Hidden in his belly, she remains linked to wisdom and devising good and evil.

l: Horae, Hesiod, the Homeric Hymns, and Homerica
s: The gold-filleted Hours are a group associated with Aphrodite. In Cyprus, they joyfully welcome her, clothe her in heavenly garments, crown and adorn her with gold, ornaments, necklaces, and jewels, then wear such jewels when they go to their father's house to join the gods' dances.

l: Eirene, Hesiod, the Homeric Hymns, and Homerica
s: has harmless laws Peace is characterized by harmless laws that the speaker wishes to follow. The speaker asks Ares to grant the boldness to abide within those laws while avoiding strife, hatred, and violent fiends of death.

l: Ares, Hesiod, the Homeric Hymns, and Homerica
s: Ares is a god and warrior defined by war: deadly, insatiable, mighty with spear and shield, golden-helmed, bronze-harnessed, and chariot-borne by blazing horses. He possesses a brazen spear, chariot, and team, and is called saviour of cities, defender of Olympus, helper of men, giver of dauntless youth, father of warlike Victory, and leader of righteous men. He is also father to Panic, Fear, Harmonia, and Cycnus. Though associated with strength, boldness, and peace maintained through courage, he is urged to restrain fury, avoid strife and hatred, and oppose cowardice. He loves war, city-sacking, shouts, and battle. With Cycnus he arms for battle against Heracles; grieving Cycnus’ death, he attacks Heracles, but Athene diverts his spear and Heracles wounds his thigh. Panic and Dread then carry him by chariot to Olympus.

l: Semele, Hesiod, the Homeric Hymns, and Homerica
s: Semele, also called Thyone, is Cadmus’s daughter and Dionysus’s mortal mother; through union with Zeus, she bears the immortal Dionysus.

l: Alcmena, Hesiod, the Homeric Hymns, and Homerica
s: Alcmena, Electryon’s daughter, leaves home for Thebes with her husband Amphitryon. Celebrated for beauty, height, wisdom, and devotion, she is loved by Zeus in a single night and bears twin sons: Heracles by Zeus and Iphiclus by Amphitryon.

l: Helios, Hesiod, the Homeric Hymns, and Homerica
s: Helios is a bright, tireless, deathless god: the son of Hyperion and Euryphaessa, a watchman of gods and men. He shines upon mortals and immortals, with dazzling rays, streaming bright locks, a far-seen face, and a golden helmet. Resting at Heaven’s highest point, he rides a golden-yoked chariot drawn by stallions down through Heaven to Ocean. From the bright upper air, he hears Persephone’s cries, witnesses her abduction, and tells Demeter that Zeus gave her to Hades.

l: Medea, Hesiod, the Homeric Hymns, and Homerica
s: Medea, Idyia’s daughter and Jason’s wife, lives in Corinth with her young sons, poisons Creon, then flees to Athens fearing his relatives. She leaves the sons at Hera Acraea’s altar; Creon’s relatives kill them and say she killed them and Creon.

l: Aeneas, Hesiod, the Homeric Hymns, and Homerica
s: Aeneas, son of Aphrodite and Anchises, is born from a goddess and a mortal. Mountain Nymphs raise him to boyhood; he is then brought to Anchises and taken to windy Ilion. He is destined to rule the Trojans, with descendants after him.

l: Cephalus, Hesiod, the Homeric Hymns, and Homerica
s: Cephalus, Deion's Athenian son, owns an inescapable hound; after accidentally killing his wife Procris, Cadmeans purify him, and he hunts the Teumesian fox.

l: Catalogue of Women, Hesiod, the Homeric Hymns, and Homerica
s: A genealogical poem containing Catalogue genealogies, cited for narratives of descent, Argonauts, Atalanta, Europa, Peleus, and Asclepius, unfolding across first, second, and third Catalogues and Great Eoiae.

l: Greeks, Hesiod, the Homeric Hymns, and Homerica
s: The Greeks gather for the expedition against Ilium and are initially scattered by a storm after attacking Teuthrania. At Tenedos, they leave Philoctetes behind in Lemnos, and at Ilium they lose Protesilaus before Achilles drives the Trojans back.

l: Pallas Athene, Hesiod, the Homeric Hymns, and Homerica
s: Pallas Athene is a goddess, daughter of Zeus, guardian and saviour of cities and people in war. Dread, bright-eyed, inventive, courageous, pure, and unbending of heart, she loves battle, shouting, war, and the sack of cities with Ares. She springs fully armed from Zeus’s immortal head, shaking Olympus, earth, and sea, then removes her heavenly armour. She is hailed for good fortune with happiness.

l: Europa, Hesiod, the Homeric Hymns, and Homerica
s: Europa, daughter of Phoenix, is carried from the mainland to Crete by Zeus as a bull, then bears Minos, Rhadamanthys, and Sarpedon to him.

l: Sarpedon, Hesiod, the Homeric Hymns, and Homerica
s: Son of Europa and Zeus, Sarpedon rules Lycia with Zeus-given honor and long life, leads Lycians to Troy, fights beside Hector, and attacks the Danaans' wall.

l: Hector, Hesiod, the Homeric Hymns, and Homerica
s: Hector kills Protesilaus when the Greeks attempt to land at Ilium.

l: Phrixus, Hesiod, the Homeric Hymns, and Homerica
s: Phrixus travels with Helle on Nephele’s immortal golden-fleeced ram, is pursued by Harpy, reaches Aeetes holding the fleece, and is received directly because of it.

l: Asclepius, Hesiod, the Homeric Hymns, and Homerica
s: Asclepius is a lord, healer of sicknesses, and son of Apollo. One tradition names Arsinoe as his mother and makes Eriopis his sibling; another says Coronis bore him in the Dotian plain. He brings great joy to men by healing sicknesses and soothing cruel pangs, and is greeted and prayed to in song.

l: marriage of Peleus and Thetis, Hesiod, the Homeric Hymns, and Homerica
s: is_attended_by gods [on Pelion] At the marriage of Peleus and Thetis, the gods gather on Mount Pelion to feast and bring gifts for Peleus. Cheiron gives Peleus an ashen spear shaft, Athena polishes it, and Hephaestus fits it with a head; Strife’s arrival at the feast begins the dispute among Hera, Athena, and Aphrodite.

l: Catalogue genealogies, Hesiod, the Homeric Hymns, and Homerica
s: is_a genealogical material [preserved in fragments attributed to Hesiod] The Catalogue genealogies preserve lines of descent among gods, heroes, kings, peoples, and places, including the families of Deucalion, Hellen, Aeolus, Lycaon, Europa, Aeacus, and Asclepius. They also record competing genealogical versions, such as different parentages for Phineus and Asclepius and differing accounts of the children of Amphion and Niobe.

l: Catalogue of the Daughters of Leucippus, Hesiod, the Homeric Hymns, and Homerica
s: represents destruction of the Cyclopes by Apollo The Catalogue of the Daughters of Leucippus represents Apollo as destroying the Cyclopes.

l: Echemus, Hesiod, the Homeric Hymns, and Homerica
s: is_married_to Timandra [as his wife] Echemus made Timandra his buxom wife.

l: Timandra, Hesiod, the Homeric Hymns, and Homerica
s: Timandra, Echemus’s buxom wife, deserts him for Phyleus and becomes Phyleus’s partner.

l: Castor, Hesiod, the Homeric Hymns, and Homerica
s: Castor is a horse-taming rider, one of the Tyndaridae and Dioscuri, born to Leda beneath Taygetus and called both a son of Zeus and a child or son of Tyndareus. He is brother to Polydeuces; together they are linked to Philoctetes and receive messages from Menelaus during the suit for Helen. Castor and Polydeuces steal cattle from Idas and Lynceus, after which Idas kills Castor. Because Castor is mortal and Polydeuces immortal, Zeus grants the brothers immortality on alternate days.

l: Polydeuces, Hesiod, the Homeric Hymns, and Homerica
s: Polydeuces is a blameless, prize-winning member of the Tyndaridae and Dioscuri, named with his brother Castor. He is presented as son of Zeus, born to Leda beneath Taygetus, yet also called son and child of Tyndareus. A rider of swift horses, he joins Castor in trying to make Philoctetes their brother and in stealing Idas and Lynceus’s cattle. After Castor is killed, Polydeuces kills Lynceus and Idas; Zeus grants the brothers immortality every other day.

l: Leda, Hesiod, the Homeric Hymns, and Homerica
s: Leda, neat-ankled and stately, is mother of Castor and Polydeuces, bearing them beneath Taygetus after the dark-clouded Son of Cronos privately bent her to his will and after lying with Zeus.

l: Tyndareus, Hesiod, the Homeric Hymns, and Homerica
s: Tyndareus, son of Oebalus and king of a bright city, angers Aphrodite by forgetting her in sacrifice; he binds Helen’s suitors by oath and lets Menelaus prevail for greatest gifts.

l: Clytaemnestra, Hesiod, the Homeric Hymns, and Homerica
s: Clytaemnestra deserts Agamemnon for Aegisthus, then murders Agamemnon together with Aegisthus.

l: suitors of Helen, Hesiod, the Homeric Hymns, and Homerica
s: swore Helen’s suitor oath [at Tyndareus’ command] The suitors of Helen came from many places, including Ithaca, Phylace, Athens, Salamis, Euboea, Crete, and elsewhere, bringing gifts or promising possessions and tribute. Tyndareus required them to swear that they would defend the marriage against anyone who took Helen by force, and Menelaus ultimately defeated them all in the suit.

l: demigods, Hesiod, the Homeric Hymns, and Homerica
s: are_children_of gods [born from unions of immortals and mortals] The demigods were the children of gods and mortal women or men. Zeus planned to destroy their race and imposed toil and sorrow upon those born from immortals and mortals.

l: Zeus’s plan to destroy the demigods, Hesiod, the Homeric Hymns, and Homerica
s: Zeus plans to mingle storm and tempest over the earth, end mortal life, and destroy demigods, preventing gods from mating with mortals and restoring their separation.

l: Iphigeneia, Hesiod, the Homeric Hymns, and Homerica
s: Iphigeneia is summoned to Aulis under the pretense that she will marry Achilles so that she can be sacrificed to Artemis. Artemis rescues her, transports her to the Tauri, and makes her immortal.

l: Eurytus, Hesiod, the Homeric Hymns, and Homerica
s: Eurytus, father of Iole and two or four sons, is linked to Heracles sacking Oechalia for Iole’s sake.

l: Meleager, Hesiod, the Homeric Hymns, and Homerica
s: Meleager, son of Oeneus and Althaea and loved by Ares, was a powerful hero with portentous fiery eyes; he slew the Calydonian boar, fought for Calydon, and was killed by Apollo.

l: Calydonian boar, Hesiod, the Homeric Hymns, and Homerica
s: is_a wild boar [destructive and tusked] The Calydonian boar was a fierce, destructive beast with gleaming tusks. Meleager slew it in high Calydon.

l: Diomedes, Hesiod, the Homeric Hymns, and Homerica
s: brings Philoctetes [from Lemnos] Diomedes brings Philoctetes from Lemnos after Helenus prophesies about the taking of Troy. He also helps Odysseus carry the Palladium out of Troy.

l: Helen’s suitor oath, Hesiod, the Homeric Hymns, and Homerica
s: Helen’s suitor oath, sworn before her marriage, bound all suitors not to act independently and to unite in punishing anyone who seized her by force.

l: marriage of Helen and Menelaus, Hesiod, the Homeric Hymns, and Homerica
s: was_won_by Menelaus [against all the other suitors through superior gifts] The marriage of Helen and Menelaus followed Menelaus’s victory over the other suitors in the contest for her hand. Menelaus prevailed because he offered the greatest gifts, and Helen later bore him Hermione and Nicostratus.

l: Calydonian boar hunt, Hesiod, the Homeric Hymns, and Homerica
s: occurred_at Calydon [Meleager killed the boar there] The Calydonian boar hunt is represented through Meleager’s killing of the fierce boar at Calydon. Meleager was later slain by Apollo while fighting the Curetes over Calydon.

l: Amphitryon, Hesiod, the Homeric Hymns, and Homerica
s: Amphitryon, a hero and gatherer of the people, kills Electryon in anger over oxen and comes to Thebes as a suppliant. Required to avenge Alcmena’s brothers, he leads a campaign against the Taphians and Teleboans, burns their villages, returns to Alcmena, and fathers Iphiclus.

l: Pylos, Hesiod, the Homeric Hymns, and Homerica
s: Pylos is the destination toward which Hermes drives Apollo’s cattle. Hermes and Apollo later return there, reach the ford of Alpheus, and find the cattle in a high-roofed byre.

l: shield-making by Hephaestus, Hesiod, the Homeric Hymns, and Homerica
s: produces Shield of Heracles [by Zeus’s will] Hephaestus makes and fits the shield at Zeus’s command. The shield’s workmanship includes precious materials and detailed figures that appear almost alive, including fighting warriors, moving animals, Perseus in flight, and scenes of human work and celebration.

l: war against Cycnus, Hesiod, the Homeric Hymns, and Homerica
s: is_fought_by Heracles [with Iolaus as charioteer] Heracles and Iolaus drive toward Cycnus and Ares after Athena gives Heracles instructions for the encounter. Cycnus refuses to withdraw, and the opposing warriors leap from their chariots and begin fighting as Zeus thunders and sends drops of blood as a battle sign.

l: Heracles and Iolaus’s victory over Cycnus, Hesiod, the Homeric Hymns, and Homerica
s: Heracles and Iolaus, aided by power Zeus gives Heracles, fight Cycnus, with Iolaus serving as charioteer and warrior. After Cycnus’ spear fails against Heracles’ shield, Heracles kills him with a thrust to the unguarded neck, and he and Iolaus receive Cycnus’ armour as spoils.

l: Cycnus’ burial, Hesiod, the Homeric Hymns, and Homerica
s: is_conducted_by Ceyx [with the people of nearby cities] Ceyx buries Cycnus, and many people gather to honour Ceyx. Anaurus, swollen by a rain-storm, later destroys Cycnus’ grave and memorial because Apollo commanded it.

l: the battle between Heracles and Ares, Hesiod, the Homeric Hymns, and Homerica
s: After Cycnus falls, Ares and Heracles charge each other; Athene deflects Ares’s spear, and Heracles wounds Ares, who is carried away from the battlefield to Olympus.

l: Marriage of Ceyx, Hesiod, the Homeric Hymns, and Homerica
s: The Marriage of Ceyx is an ancient poem attributed to Hesiod, though disputed, describing Heracles seeking water after leaving the Argo, his stay with Ceyx at Trachis, and domestic preparations.

l: The Great Eoiae, Hesiod, the Homeric Hymns, and Homerica
s: is_a epic poem The Great Eoiae is cited for genealogies and stories involving Argos, Epidaurus, Heracles, Telamon, Polycaon, Endymion, Melampus, Phineus, and the children of Phrixus. It tells how Hermes stole cattle and changed Battus into a rock after Battus revealed where the cattle were hidden.

l: Battus, Hesiod, the Homeric Hymns, and Homerica
s: Battus lives on a rock, recognizes stolen cattle, accepts Hermes’ rewards for secrecy then disclosure, and is transformed into a rock for being double-tongued.

l: Apollo's cattle, Hesiod, the Homeric Hymns, and Homerica
s: Apollo’s divine cattle are fifty loud-lowing kine kept in Pieria. Hermes steals them from Apollo’s meadow, reverses their hoofprints, drives them by a winding route toward the Alpheus and Pylos, hides them in a byre, feeds them, and sacrifices two. Apollo and Hermes recover them; Hermes agrees to graze them for abundant reproduction.

l: The Melampodia, Hesiod, the Homeric Hymns, and Homerica
s: is_a poem The Melampodia includes accounts of Calchas's contest with Mopsus, Teiresias's long life and prophetic experiences, and the deaths of Calchas and Amphilochus. It also contains passages concerning feasting, omens, Mares, Mantes, Iphiclus, Phylacus, and Chalcis.

l: Mopsus, Hesiod, the Homeric Hymns, and Homerica
s: Mopsus, Manto's son, is a seer greater than Calchas, proven by correctly counting a wild fig-tree's figs.

l: Manto, Hesiod, the Homeric Hymns, and Homerica
s: Manto, daughter of Teiresias, is sent by the Epigoni to Delphi as spoil. Following Apollo’s oracle, she meets and marries Rhacius, comes with him to Colophon, and weeps there over Thebes’s destruction.

l: gods, Hesiod, the Homeric Hymns, and Homerica
s: The gods are blessed, deathless immortals who inhabit Olympus, possess heavenly food and ambrosia, and respond to divine actions with fear or honor. Most are subject to Aphrodite in love and desire, though Athene, Artemis, and Hestia resist her. They welcome the adorned Aphrodite, marvel at her beauty, and each prays to wed her; Zeus arranges her meeting with Anchises and Hermes carries messages. Later, Hermes shows them Pan, whose sight delights their hearts, and they call him Pan.

l: Io, Hesiod, the Homeric Hymns, and Homerica
s: Io, daughter of Peiren and priestess of Hera, is seduced by Zeus; after Hera discovers this, Zeus changes her into a white cow, and Hera sets Argus to watch her.

l: Argus, Hesiod, the Homeric Hymns, and Homerica
s: Argus is a great, strong watcher and herdsman set by Hera over Io, with four ever-wakeful eyes; he watches tirelessly until Hermes slays him.

l: Linus, Hesiod, the Homeric Hymns, and Homerica
s: Linus, the very lovely son of Urania, is skilled in all manner of wisdom and is invoked and bewailed by singers and harpers at the beginnings and endings of feasts and dances.

l: the gods of Olympus, Hesiod, the Homeric Hymns, and Homerica
s: The deathless gods are honored through the Eleusinian Mysteries’ rites and offerings. They repeatedly visit Demeter with gifts and offered rights but cannot end her anger. They later receive Demeter and Persephone among them, though Persephone is absent for one-third of the year, and serve as the community governing honors, renown, and Hermes’s messenger role.

l: mountain Nymphs, Hesiod, the Homeric Hymns, and Homerica
s: Mountain Nymphs are divine, long-lived beings born from daughters of Hecaterus, neither mortal nor immortal. Living on Mount Ida, they raise Aeneas, eat heavenly food and dance among immortals; their lives begin and end linked to trees.

l: ships, Hesiod, the Homeric Hymns, and Homerica
s: Poseidon is described as a saviour of ships. The hymn asks him to help those who voyage in ships.

l: Nysa, Hesiod, the Homeric Hymns, and Homerica
s: Nysa is a very high, richly wooded mountain in far-off Phoenice near the streams of Aegyptus. It has shrines, dells, and a sweet-smelling cave. Dionysus is truly born there and grows up in its cave under the Nymphs’ care.

l: Dionysus's birth, Hesiod, the Homeric Hymns, and Homerica
s: Different accounts place Dionysus's birth at Dracanum, windy Icarus, Naxos, the river Alpheus, and Thebes, but the hymn says these accounts are false. It states that Zeus gave birth to Dionysus secretly and far from men, at Nysa.

l: holy song, Hesiod, the Homeric Hymns, and Homerica
s: is_called_to_mind by singers [when Dionysus is not forgotten] The singers invoke Dionysus as they begin and end a strain. They say that no one who forgets him may call holy song to mind.

l: Celeus, Hesiod, the Homeric Hymns, and Homerica
s: Celeus, wise ruler of fragrant Eleusis and father in Metaneira’s household, receives disguised Demeter and gathers the people to build her temple and altar.

l: Metaneira, Hesiod, the Homeric Hymns, and Homerica
s: Metaneira, Celeus’s wife and Demophoon’s mother, employs Doso as nurse, then interrupts Demeter’s fire ritual, ending Demophoon’s possible immortality.

l: Callidice, Hesiod, the Homeric Hymns, and Homerica
s: Callidice, queen of the Thesprotians, marries Odysseus; after her death, Polypoetes succeeds while Odysseus returns to Ithaca.

l: Iambe, Hesiod, the Homeric Hymns, and Homerica
s: cheers Demeter [with quips and jest] Iambe gives the disguised Demeter a jointed seat covered with a silvery fleece. Through quips and jokes, she makes the grieving goddess smile, laugh, and regain some cheer.

l: Demophoon, Hesiod, the Homeric Hymns, and Homerica
s: Demophoon, late-born son of Celeus and Metaneira, is nursed by Demeter and grows like an immortal until Metaneira’s interruption leaves him mortal.

l: the golden chariot, Hesiod, the Homeric Hymns, and Homerica
s: Hades uses his golden chariot and immortal horses to seize Persephone and carry her to his realm. After Helios speaks to Demeter, he calls his own horses and drives his chariot away.

l: kykeon draught, Hesiod, the Homeric Hymns, and Homerica
s: The kykeon draught is prepared for Demeter from meal, water, and soft mint after she refuses red wine. Demeter drinks it in order to observe the sacrament.

l: Demeter’s temple, Hesiod, the Homeric Hymns, and Homerica
s: is_built_at Eleusis [on a rising hillock below the city] Demeter commands the people of Eleusis to build her a great temple below the city and its sheer wall, on a rising hillock above Callichorus. Celeus summons the people, who obey and construct it.

l: Demeter’s altar, Hesiod, the Homeric Hymns, and Homerica
s: is_built_at Eleusis [below the temple] Demeter commands that an altar be built beneath her temple on the rising hillock above Callichorus. Celeus orders the people to build it, and they carry out his command.

l: abduction of Persephone, Hesiod, the Homeric Hymns, and Homerica
s: The abduction of Persephone is an event in which, as Persephone gathers flowers with other maidens, the earth opens beneath her. With Zeus’s permission and plan, Hades emerges in a golden chariot, seizes her against her will, and carries her away to the underworld as she cries for her father.

l: Demeter’s search for Persephone, Hesiod, the Homeric Hymns, and Homerica
s: lasts nine days [across earth with flaming torches] Demeter searches for Persephone across the earth and sea for nine days, carrying flaming torches and asking gods and mortals for news. On the tenth day, Hecate directs her to Helios, who tells her what happened.

l: Demeter’s mourning, Hesiod, the Homeric Hymns, and Homerica
s: causes Demeter [she abstains from ambrosia, nectar, and bathing] Demeter grieves intensely after Persephone’s abduction, tears at her hair, casts off her cloak, and refuses ambrosia, nectar, food, and drink. Her grief and anger lead her to avoid the gods and withdraw among mortals.

l: Demeter’s disguise as Doso, Hesiod, the Homeric Hymns, and Homerica
s: takes_place_at Eleusis [as an apparently mortal old woman] Demeter disguises herself as an old mortal woman named Doso and claims to have escaped pirates from Crete. In this form, she seeks work and enters Celeus’s household.

l: Demeter’s nursing of Demophoon, Hesiod, the Homeric Hymns, and Homerica
s: includes ambrosia [daily anointing] As Doso, Demeter takes Demophoon into her care and nurses him. She feeds him ambrosia by day, breathes sweetly upon him, and tends him at night in the fire.

l: attempt to make Demophoon immortal, Hesiod, the Homeric Hymns, and Homerica
s: Demeter attempts to make Demophoon deathless and ageless by placing him in fire at night, but Metaneira interrupts; Demophoon remains mortal yet gains lasting honour.
